summary: Specifies the Host Monitoring Protocol, used to collect information from various kinds of hosts in the Internet. Designers of communications software were encouraged to consider it for monitoring their systems. This RFC is historic.

eli5.summary: A way for a central computer to collect health reports from many other computers.

subtitle: Centralized host monitoring through a polling-based transport protocol.

tldr.problem: System administrators need a way to collect monitoring data from many hosts across a network, including alerts about errors and statistics about traffic.
tldr.mechanism: HMP provides a polling-based protocol where a central monitoring station sends queries to hosts, and hosts respond with status, trap alerts, or statistical data, using a simple header with sequence numbers and checksums.
tldr.outcome: RFC 869 was marked Historic and is no longer used; modern network monitoring uses SNMP instead.

today: RFC 869 is marked Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1067 and later superseded entirely by the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), which became the standard for network monitoring and is still widely used today. HMP's polling-based approach and simple header format gave way to SNMP's more sophisticated agent-manager model and MIB (Management Information Base) system.

sections.title: What is HMP
sections.content:
The Host Monitoring Protocol is a network transport protocol used to collect information from computers spread across an internet. It was designed so that a central monitoring center could gather data from different types of hosts, including servers, workstations, terminal concentrators, packet switches, and gateways.

HMP is transaction-oriented (also called connection-less), meaning each request-response pair stands alone, with no ongoing connection setup. It runs on top of IP, using protocol number 20, and was built around the principle that intelligence should live in the monitoring center, not scattered in every monitored host.
sections.eli5: HMP is a way for one computer (the monitor) to ask many other computers 'What is your status?' and get answers back. Each question and answer works on its own, like sending postcards.

sections.title: How HMP Works
sections.content:
HMP collects three kinds of data. Traps are unsolicited alerts: when something happens (an error, a crash, a threshold crossed), the host immediately sends a trap message to the monitor. Status messages describe the current state of a host; the monitor requests status by sending a poll, and the host responds with its latest state. Statistical data is collected over time periods; the monitor polls for it and the host responds with counts and measurements.

The protocol is built on polling. The monitor sends a poll request specifying which kind of data it wants (trap, status, or statistics, and of what type). The monitored host receives the poll, checks that the system type and password match, and responds with the requested data or an error message if it cannot provide what was requested. If the monitor does not receive a response within a reasonable time, it simply polls again. This allows the protocol to work even if some messages are lost.

The monitor maintains separate sequence numbers for each host, used to match responses to polls and to detect duplicate messages. Each message also includes a one's complement checksum for error detection.
sections.eli5: The monitor asks each host three kinds of questions: 'Alert me if something breaks!' (traps), 'What is your status right now?' (status), and 'Count the traffic you saw.' (statistics). If the host doesn't answer, the monitor just asks again.

sections.title: Protocol Messages
sections.content:
All HMP messages begin with a 10-octet (80-bit) header followed by optional data. The header contains:

  • System Type (1 octet): identifies the kind of machine (host, IMP, TAC, gateway, etc.). Defined types range from 1 to 12.
  • Message Type (1 octet): indicates the message class. Values 1-7 are for unsolicited or response messages (trap, status, throughput, traffic matrix, parameters, routing, call accounting). Values 100-102 are for monitoring center messages (poll, error, control acknowledgment).
  • Port Number (1 octet): reserved for multiplexing to different processes; currently unused.
  • Control Flag (1 octet): bit 15 is the 'More' bit, used to indicate that more data is available to poll for.
  • Sequence Number (2 octets): incremented each time a message of that type is sent, allowing the monitor to detect lost and duplicate messages.
  • Password or Returned Sequence Number (2 octets): when polling, carries the password for authentication; in responses, echoes the sequence number from the poll.
  • Checksum (2 octets): one's complement checksum of all 16-bit words in the header and data.

Polling messages include an R-Message Type and R-Subtype field identifying what kind of response is requested, and may carry data when setting parameters on the host.
sections.eli5: Each message has a small header with labels (who sent it, what kind of message, a number to track it) and maybe some data attached. The header also has a checksum to make sure the message wasn't scrambled.

sections.title: Types of Messages
sections.content:
From the monitoring center, the protocol defines three message types. Type 100 (Poll) asks a host to send trap, status, or statistics data, or to accept control data. Type 101 (Error) is sent by the host when it receives a poll it cannot handle (unknown message type, unsupported subtype, invalid parameters, or the machine is in loader mode). Type 102 (Control Acknowledgment) is the host's response after receiving control data from the monitor.

From monitored entities, message types 1-7 carry the actual monitoring data. Type 1 (Trap) reports spontaneous events. Type 2 (Status) describes current state. Type 3 (Throughput) carries traffic statistics. Type 4 (Host Traffic Matrix) shows communication patterns. Type 5 (Parameters) returns configured values. Type 6 (Routing) provides routing information. Type 7 (Call Accounting) is for accounting data.

The RFC includes detailed message formats for monitoring IMPs (Interface Message Processors, used in the ARPANET), TACs (Terminal Access Controllers), and gateways, showing the specific fields and counters each type provides.
sections.eli5: The monitor sends three kinds of requests: 'Send me data' (poll), 'I sent you bad data' (error), and 'Did you apply my settings?' (acknowledgment). Hosts send back alerts, status, counts of packets, and other measurements.
